questions.problem: The parabola $y={x}^{2}+2x+2$ and the line $y=2-2x$ intersect at the points $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ and $({x}_{2},{y}_{2}),$ where ${x}_{1}<{x}_{2}.$ What is the value of ${y}_{1}+{y}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to solve the following system consisting of the equations of the curves:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+2x+2 \\ y=2-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x+2 & =2-2x \\ {x}^{2}+4x & =0 \\ x(x+4) & =0 \\ x & =-4,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}_{1}<{x}_{2},$ the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points are ${x}_{1}=-4$ and ${x}_{2}=0.$ 

To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we plug these values into either curve. Let's choose the line since it's simpler.

- Substituting ${x}_{1}=-4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =2-2{x}_{1} \\  & =2-2(-4) \\  & =10,\end{aligned}
$$

so one point of intersection is $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-4,10).$

- Substituting ${x}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & =2-2{x}_{2} \\  & =2-2(0) \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the other point of intersection is $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(0,2).$

Therefore, ${y}_{1}=10,\,{y}_{2}=2,$ and

$$
{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}=10+2=12.
$$

questions.problem: Given that the line $y=x+k$ does **not** intersect the parabola $y={x}^{2}+1,$ what is the range of possible values of $k?$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine whether the line $y=x+k$ intersects the parabola $y={x}^{2}+1,$ we need to solve the following system of equations for the two curves:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+1 \\ y=x+k\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and writing in standard form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+1 & =x+k \\ {x}^{2}-x+1-k & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve this equation using the quadratic formula with $a=1,\,b=-1,$ and $c=1-k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-(-1)\pm \sqrt{(-1)^{2}-4(1)(1-k)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{1-4+4k}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{4k-3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the line and parabola do not intersect, our quadratic equation must have no real solutions; hence, the expression inside the square root must be negative.
Setting up and solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4k-3 & <0 \\ 4k & <3 \\ k & <\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range of possible values of $k$ is $k<\frac{3}{4}.$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+5x-1 \\ y=-2x-13\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+5x-1 & =-2x-13 \\ {x}^{2}+7x+12 & =0 \\ (x+4)(x+3) & =0 \\ x & =-4,-3.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =-2{x}_{1}-13 \\  & =-2(-4)-13 \\  & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

so one point of intersection is $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-4,-5).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & =-2{x}_{2}-13 \\  & =-2(-3)-13 \\  & =-7,\end{aligned}
$$

The parabola $y={x}^{2}+5x+1$ and the line $y=3x$ intersect at the point $P.$ Find the coordinates of $P.$

The coordinates of $P$ are
$(${{field-1}}$,$

questions.worked_solution:
We need to solve the following system consisting of the equations of the curves:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+5x+1 \\ y=3x\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+5x+1 & =3x \\ {x}^{2}+5x+1-3x & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x+1 & =0 \\ (x+1)(x+1) & =0 \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $x$-coordinate of the intersection point is $x=-1.$

To find the $y$-coordinate of the intersection point, we plug this value into either curve. Let's choose the equation of the line. Substituting $x=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x \\  & =3(-1) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only point of intersection is $(-1,-3).$

questions.worked_solution:
We need to solve the following system consisting of the equations of the curves:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+x+4 \\ y=5x\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+x+4 & =5x \\ {x}^{2}-4x+4 & =0 \\ (x-2)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $x$-coordinate of the intersection point is $x=2.$

To find the $y$-coordinate of the intersection point, we plug this value into either curve. Let's choose the equation of the line. Substituting $x=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5x \\  & =5(2) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only point of intersection is $(2,10).$
